content: Sweet Birch, scientifically known as Betula lenta, is also referred to by several other names, including Black Birch, Cherry Birch, Mahogany Birch, River Birch, and Spice Birch. This species of birch is native to the eastern regions of North America, ranging from southern Maine westward to southern Ontario and southern Michigan, and extending southward along the Appalachian Mountains to northern Georgia. This tree is classified as a medium-sized deciduous species, typically growing to a height of approximately 20 meters, with a trunk diameter that can reach up to 60 centimeters. Unlike most other birches, the bark of Sweet Birch is rough in texture and exhibits a dark blackish-brown coloration. It tends to crack into irregular, scaly plates. When the twigs are scraped, they emit a strong aroma reminiscent of oil of wintergreen. The leaves of Sweet Birch are arranged alternately along the branches. They are ovate in shape, measuring between 5 to 10 centimeters in length and 4 to 8 centimeters in width, with finely serrated edges. The flowers of this tree are wind-pollinated and appear as catkins. Male catkins are pendulous and measure 3 to 6 centimeters in length, while female catkins are erect. The fruit, which matures in the fall, consists of numerous tiny winged seeds that are tightly packed between the bracts of the catkin. Historically, Sweet Birch was commercially utilized for the production of oil of wintergreen before the advent of modern industrial synthesis. The tree's name reflects the distinctive wintergreen scent of its shoots. The sap of Sweet Birch begins to flow approximately one month later than maple sap and does so at a much faster rate. The trees can be tapped in a manner similar to maple trees, but the sap must be collected about three times more frequently. Birch sap can be boiled in the same way as maple sap to produce syrup, although the resulting syrup has a stronger flavor, akin to molasses. Additionally, the leaves of Sweet Birch serve as a food source for certain species of lepidopteran caterpillars. For further details, one can refer to the list of Lepidoptera that feed on birches.
